questions.q: What browser feature makes DOM clobbering possible?
o: The fact that browsers execute inline event handlers on all elements
The HTML specification's Named Access on the Window object, which exposes elements with id or name attributes as properties of window
A bug in V8's property lookup optimizations
The same-origin policy's exception for element references
questions.x: The HTML spec (section 7.3.3) requires browsers to create window.foo for any element with id='foo'. This is a legacy feature from the 1990s web, preserved for backward compatibility, and it enables clobbering without any script execution.
questions.h: This is a specified behavior, not a browser bug. Where in the HTML spec would you find the rule that creates window properties from element IDs?

questions.q: What does it mean to 'clobber' a variable?
o: To delete it from the global scope with delete window.x
To overwrite an existing JavaScript variable by creating an HTML element whose id matches the variable name
To shadow it with a local variable inside a function
To freeze it with Object.freeze() so it cannot be changed
questions.x: When JavaScript code reads window.config or just config, and an attacker can inject an element with id='config', the element replaces the original variable value. The original value is 'clobbered' by the DOM element reference.
questions.h: The word clobber means to hit or overwrite forcefully. What does the attacker create in the DOM to overwrite the JavaScript variable?

questions.q: How is a two-level property chain (e.g., config.key) clobbered using nested anchor elements?
o: The outer anchor's href clobbers config, the inner anchor's href clobbers config.key
An anchor with id='config' creates window.config, a child anchor with name='key' is accessible as window.config.key via the element's HTMLCollection named access
Two nested anchors merge their id attributes into a dot-separated string
Nesting anchors is invalid HTML, so the parser creates a flat structure the clobbering uses
questions.x: When window.config is an anchor element, accessing window.config.key looks for a property called key on that element. If the element has a child with name='key', the browser returns it via named access, creating the two-level chain.
questions.h: Once you have window.config as an anchor element, you need window.config.key to return something you control. What does accessing a named property on a DOM element do if a child element has that name attribute?

questions.q: Why can anchor elements be effective clobbering gadgets beyond just their id attribute?
o: Anchor elements are the only tags browsers allow with both id and name attributes
Anchor elements have a href property that can be set to a javascript: URI or any other URL, giving the attacker control over a string value that code might use as a URL or script source
Anchor elements are rendered outside the shadow DOM, giving them elevated privileges
Anchor elements bypass DOMPurify's parser because they are self-closing
questions.x: Accessing window.config where config is an anchor returns the element. Accessing window.config.href returns the anchor's href value. If the application uses that value as a script src or navigation target, the attacker controls the URL.
questions.h: DOM elements have properties beyond just their tag. What property of an anchor element represents its destination URL, and what could an attacker put there?

questions.q: What DOMPurify configuration option removes id and name attributes to prevent clobbering?
o: FORCE_BODY: true
FORBID_ATTR: ['id', 'name']
ALLOWED_TAGS: []
WHOLE_DOCUMENT: false
questions.x: FORBID_ATTR removes specified attributes from all allowed elements. Stripping id and name prevents any injected element from participating in named access on window, eliminating the clobbering surface.
questions.h: DOMPurify has an option that takes a list of attribute names to remove from all sanitized HTML. What is it called?
